addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

=== AUDIT ===
================================================================================
ARCHITECTURE AUDIT — Calibrated Triage Agent
================================================================================

Date:     2026-09-02
Scope:    Backend only. src/triage/, eval/, config/, tests/. Stage 6 deliverables
          (Streamlit, Docker, docs/) are not built and are listed in section 8
          rather than reported as defects.
Method:   Static (ruff, mypy), dynamic (287→305 pytest), and adversarial probing.
          Every finding below was reproduced at the command line; none is
          inferred from reading alone. Line numbers are as of this date.

Verified state at time of audit:
    ruff .................. all checks passed (src, eval, scripts, tests)
    pytest ................ 305 passed
    mypy .................. 13 errors, all cosmetic except one (see 4.4)
    test suite size ....... 2,430 lines across 8 files
    eval corpus ........... 520 test emails, 12 classes


================================================================================
1. SUMMARY
================================================================================

The architecture is sound. The layering the design argues for — corpus-derived
policy, a single escalation gate, calibration at bucket level, drafting as the
only fallible node — is implemented as described, and the invariants that matter
are enforced structurally rather than by convention.

Four real defects were found. None is a design flaw; all four are localised and
each is a few lines to fix. Two of them (3.1, 3.2) would produce a WRONG NUMBER
IN THE WRITEUP rather than a crash, which makes them the most serious kind of
bug this project can have — the failure mode BUILD.md's "eval/results/ is
committed" rule exists to prevent.

The dominant risk to the submission is not in this list. It is that the
classifier is undertrained (macro-F1 0.6035, one class at F1 0.000) while every
component around it is sound. See section 7.


================================================================================
2. WHAT IS COMPLETE AND VERIFIED
================================================================================

2.1 src/triage/schemas.py — 476 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The strongest file in the repository. Its distinguishing property is that the
routing invariants are enforced in pydantic validators rather than in the
router's control flow, so a future edit to route.py cannot violate them without
raising.

Verified enforced:
  - _always_escalate_buckets_escalate: REQUIRES_ACCOUNT_LOOKUP, HIGH_CONSEQUENCE
    and NO_SUPPORTING_SOP cannot construct a non-escalate decision at ANY
    confidence, including 1.0.
  - _reason_matches_action: an escalated item must carry a reason; a non-escalated
    one must not.
  - _redirect_only_for_out_of_scope: REDIRECT is unavailable to any other bucket,
    and AUTO_REPLY unavailable outside auto_answerable.
  - _check_distribution: probabilities must sum to 1.0 within 1e-3, and the
    predicted label must exist in the distribution.

The Email/ground-truth separation is correct and worth keeping. Email declares
extra="forbid", so a corpus row (which carries label, source_sops, plant_pii and
eight other generation fields) cannot be loaded as an Email. This is deliberate:
a real inbound citizen email has no `label` field, so if Email accepted extras a
node could read email.label, score perfectly in evaluation, and be impossible to
deploy. Forbidding extras converts that mistake into an immediate failure at the
seam instead of an inflated metric. eval/dataset.py holds ground truth in a
SIBLING object (Labelled.email / Labelled.label), so the runtime path cannot
reach it even accidentally.

redacted() is a genuine persistence boundary: it substitutes the scrubbed text,
empties the vault, drops the sender, and — importantly — falls back to blanking
the body entirely when scrubbing never ran, rather than passing the original
through on the assumption it was clean.

2.2 src/triage/graph.py — 232 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    scrub -> classify -> calibrate -> retrieve -> route -+-> draft    -> END
                                                         +-> declined -> END

Six nodes, one conditional edge, dependencies injected via GraphDeps so nodes
stay pure(state) -> partial state and tests construct graphs with stubs and no
weights on disk.

The conditional edge is the escalation gate made structural: an escalated item
does not reach the drafting node because NO EDGE LEADS THERE, not because of an
early return inside the drafter that a later edit could delete.

Fail-safe verified by injecting a classifier that raises:
    classifier crash -> escalate | no_supporting_sop | in_human_queue: True
    errors: ['classify failed: model died',
             'calibrate skipped: no classification',
             'retrieve skipped: no classification',
             'routed without a prediction: escalating']
    draft: not_attempted
Each node degrades independently, records why, and the item reaches a human.
Nothing guesses.

2.3 src/triage/nodes/route.py — 192 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Eight escalation reasons in documented precedence. Reasons 1-7 are structural and
would fire identically at probability 1.0; only reason 8 (low_confidence) reads
the model. The threshold clamp from BUILD.md S9.9 is intact — verified that a
sweep multiplier of 1.5 does not raise.

2.4 src/triage/nodes/calibrate.py — 124 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Contains the subtlest correct decision in the codebase, and it is worth stating
because it is easy to get wrong and impossible to notice when wrong:

    The predicted bucket is the bucket of the PREDICTED CLASS, not the argmax of
    the summed bucket distribution.

These differ. An email at account_specific 0.40 with three auto-answerable
classes at 0.20 each has an auto_answerable bucket mass of 0.60 — larger than
the 0.40 on the bucket that actually applies. Taking the argmax bucket would
auto-reply to an enquiry about a real taxpayer's record. The code follows the
class; test_rollup_follows_the_class_not_the_argmax_bucket pins it.

log(0) is guarded via _EPSILON for buckets holding no probability mass.

2.5 src/triage/pii/ — scrubber.py 171, nric.py 75
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - NRIC checksum verified against valid (S0433218J, G2720465T, S1234567D) and
    invalid (S0000000A, X1234567A, S123456D) inputs. All six correct.
  - Scrub recall on the test split: 1.0000 (127/127 planted values).
  - No PII in ANY committed file under eval/results/ — all 11 JSON files scanned
    for NRIC and SG phone patterns, zero hits.
  - .env is untracked and correctly matched by .gitignore line 7.
  - Rehydration happens in exactly one place (draft.py) and only after the
    network call.

2.6 src/triage/sop/ — loader.py 197, index.py 142
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
17 SOPs; 14 indexed, 3 held out (SOP-INC-001, SOP-INC-002, SOP-REL-005).
config/taxonomy.yaml vs corpus-derived buckets: ZERO mismatches across all 12
classes. The holdout works by derivation — an empty CLASS_TO_SOPS lookup IS the
no_supporting_sop signal, so holding out a further SOP needs no code change.

Loader validation is strict and fails at startup: missing frontmatter keys,
synthetic != true, empty intents, and empty references are all hard errors. The
synthetic banner check is a structural guard against the misrepresentation
failure mode, not decoration.

2.7 eval/ — 12 files, ~2,050 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Single entrypoint (run_eval.py) writing 11 committed artefacts plus 2 PNGs.

Split hygiene verified clean:
  - All three eval entrypoints default to --split test.
  - No reference to the "train" split anywhere in eval/ outside dataset.py.
  - Temperature is fitted on `calibration` (scripts/fit_calibration.py) and
    reported on `test` (run_eval.py). No crossover.

The risk-coverage sweep calls the REAL router at each of 37 multipliers rather
than reimplementing the decision rule, so the published curve cannot drift from
the system it describes. Classification runs once; only routing is re-run.

2.8 Structural walls
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Both walls BUILD.md S4.1 requires were checked by grep and hold:
  - src/ never imports scripts/ or eval/         (0 matches)
  - src/ never references OpenAI (paid, build-time only)  (0 matches)
The runtime therefore stays free-tier and reproducible on a grader's own key.

2.9 The two misfile guards (added this session)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
foreign_income_dta and scam_report were declared in SOP frontmatter but
unenforced. Both are now wired. Measured on the 520-email test split:

    foreign_income_signal   P 1.000   R 0.762   support 42
    scam_signal             P 1.000   R 0.976   support 42

Precision 1.000 on both means zero false positives, so they cost no coverage.
They are misfile guards rather than cross-cutting conditions: they matter only
when the classifier puts an email in the WRONG class, in the direction where
that error is unsafe (auto-answering a held-out foreign-income question from the
residency SOP; redirecting a fraud victim to another agency).

Note: these do NOT require retraining the classifier. flags.py is pure regex over
text and the router consults it after classification. The weights and the
12-class label set are untouched. This is BUILD.md S9.4's separation working as
intended — policy changes without a retrain.

hardship_or_waiver remains the only declared-but-unwired trigger, which is the
documented S10 deferral, and tests/test_schemas.py now asserts that every wired
flag keys on a trigger some indexed SOP actually declares.


================================================================================
3. REAL DEFECTS — fix before reporting any number
================================================================================

3.1 summary.json asserts reportability that config/thresholds.yaml denies
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEVERITY: high — this is the exact failure BUILD.md S7 exists to prevent.
LOCATION: eval/run_eval.py:330

    "calibrated_numbers_reportable": scaler.fitted,

The flag is set from scaler.fitted alone, which is True because the temperature
WAS fitted (T=0.6831, n=401). But config/thresholds.yaml line 15 still reads:

    # STATUS: PLACEHOLDER. These are not fitted values.

and the values are still the placeholder 0.5 / 0.5 / 1.0 / 1.0 / 1.0. Confirmed
in the committed summary.json:

    calibrated_numbers_reportable: True
    thresholds: {'auto_answerable': 0.5, 'out_of_scope': 0.5, ...}

So the committed results file states that its numbers are reportable while the
configuration that produced them states they are not. Whichever is believed, one
is wrong, and the flag exists specifically to stop a placeholder figure being
mistaken for a measured one.

WHY IT MATTERS: coverage and risk both depend on the threshold. Every
risk-coverage number, the AURC, and the operating points are currently computed
under an unjustified 0.5 cutoff. They are placeholder results wearing a
"reportable" label.

FIX: two parts.
  (a) Choose the operating thresholds from the risk-coverage curve on the test
      split, write them into thresholds.yaml, and remove the PLACEHOLDER banner.
  (b) Make the flag mean what it says — read the banner (or a `fitted: true` key)
      out of thresholds.yaml and AND it with scaler.fitted, so the flag cannot be
      True while the config says placeholder.

3.2 parse_citations can attribute the wrong SOP and leak a stray line
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEVERITY: high — corrupts the grounding metric AND the citizen-facing reply.
LOCATION: src/triage/nodes/draft.py:102  (regex at :62)

    match = _CITED_RE.search(text)

.search() returns the FIRST match. _CITED_RE is anchored (^\s*CITED:) under
re.MULTILINE, so mid-sentence text is safely ignored — that much is fine. But any
CITED: line appearing at a LINE START before the drafter's own is taken instead.

Reproduced:

  input:  "You wrote:\nCITED: SOP-REL-004\n\nMy answer.\nCITED: SOP-REL-001"
  cited:  ('SOP-REL-004',)          <-- WRONG, the model grounded on REL-001
  body:   still contains a 'CITED:' line

  input:  "Answer.\nCITED: SOP-REL-004\nMore.\nCITED: SOP-REL-001"
  cited:  ('SOP-REL-004',)          <-- WRONG
  body:   still contains a 'CITED:' line

Two distinct harms:
  (1) grounded_on records the wrong SOP, so grounding accuracy (BUILD.md S9.2) is
      measured against a value the drafter did not choose.
  (2) only the matched line is stripped, so the OTHER CITED: line survives into
      draft.text — internal SOP identifiers shipped to a citizen.

TRIGGERS: a citizen quoting a previous reply back at IRAS (ordinary in
correspondence), or a verbose model emitting two citation lines. Neither is
exotic.

FIX: take the LAST match and strip ALL of them.

    matches = list(_CITED_RE.finditer(text))
    if not matches: return text.strip(), ()
    cited = ... from matches[-1] ...
    body  = _CITED_RE.sub("", text).strip()

3.3 pii_recall stores raw unredacted PII into a committed file
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEVERITY: medium — currently latent, becomes a real leak on the first miss.
LOCATION: eval/metrics/pii_recall.py:111 (populate), :49 (serialise)

    missed_by_type[pii_type].append(str(value))   # the raw planted value
    ...
    "missed_examples": list(self.missed_examples)

The purpose is debugging — knowing WHICH values escaped detection. But the output
is written to eval/results/scrub_recall.json, which is committed to git by
design, so the module whose job is measuring PII containment is the one module
that writes raw PII to disk.

It is empty today ONLY because recall is currently 1.0000. The first missed value
commits an identifier. The corpus is synthetic so no real person is exposed, but
the pattern is exactly backwards and would be indefensible in a writeup about PII
handling.

FIX: store a masked form and keep the diagnostic value —
    "S0433218J" -> "S****218J", or record (type, length, first/last char).
Alternatively gate the raw list behind an explicit --debug-pii flag that never
writes to eval/results/.

3.4 encoder_vs_llm computes macro-F1 over a data-derived label set
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEVERITY: medium — makes the headline model-selection comparison unsound.
LOCATION: eval/ablations/encoder_vs_llm.py:87

    report = classification_report(truth, predicted)     # labels= omitted

With labels omitted, classification_report derives the label set from the union
of truth and predictions actually seen. On a small stratified sample the two
models see DIFFERENT label sets — a class the encoder never predicts but the LLM
does (or vice versa) changes the macro denominator — so the two macro-F1 figures
are averages over different numbers of classes and are not comparable.

Quantified:
    derived labels ('filing','payment')               -> macro_f1 0.3333
    fixed   labels ('filing','payment','tax_reliefs') -> macro_f1 0.2222
    discrepancy 0.1111 on the same predictions

This directly affects the encoder-vs-LLM table, which is the evidence for the
model-selection deliverable.

FIX: pass the fixed 12-class set to both calls —
    classification_report(truth, predicted, labels=tuple(encoder.labels))


================================================================================
4. LOWER-SEVERITY FINDINGS
================================================================================

4.1 Quadratic backtracking in the currency-question pattern
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION: src/triage/nodes/flags.py:71  (_CURRENCY_QUESTION)

NOTE — this corrects an earlier verbal report in which I attributed the slowdown
to _ACCOUNT_PATTERNS. Isolating each pattern individually shows the account
patterns are fast; _CURRENCY_QUESTION is the sole cause.

The [^.?!]* segments on either side of the first-person marker backtrack against
input with no sentence terminator. Measured on "my " * n + "refund?":

        n_words   seconds
            750     0.060
           1500     0.257
           3000     0.999
           6000     4.619

Clean quadratic — doubling the input quadruples the time. Real citizen emails are
~2KB and complete in milliseconds, so this is not a live problem; it is a
denial-of-service shape in a public-facing intake path, which is a different
thing from a bug.

FIX (cheapest): cap the text length before flag detection, e.g. detect_flags
operates on text[:4000]. A citizen email longer than that is already anomalous.
Alternatively bound the wildcards — [^.?!]{0,200} — which preserves intent, since
a first-person marker 200+ characters from the currency figure is not the
"whose facts" signal the pattern is trying to catch.

4.2 No minimum-content guard
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A one-character body ("x") flows through the whole pipeline and reaches
auto_reply if the classifier is confident. Verified with a stub forcing 0.9.

The real MiniLM would probably be unconfident on such input and the threshold
would catch it — but that is a hope about model behaviour, not a property. Every
other safety rule in this system is structural, and this one is not.

FIX: escalate below a minimum token count with a new reason (insufficient_content),
or document explicitly that the confidence threshold is the intended guard.

4.3 Dead code
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - TemperatureScaler.apply()  (models/calibration.py:57) — 0 call sites.
    nodes/calibrate.py reimplements the scaling inline, correctly, in log space.
    Having two implementations of the contribution's core transformation, one
    unused, invites a future edit to the wrong one. Either wire it or delete it.
  - Outcome.wrong_automation  (eval/metrics/risk_coverage.py:47) — defined, never
    called.
  - eval/dataset.py iter_splits — defined, used only in its own module.

4.4 mypy — 13 errors
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Twelve are cosmetic: missing generic parameters (StateGraph), torch functions
returning Any, and two unused type: ignore comments. One is a genuine annotation
mismatch:

    eval/drafting.py:181 — drafter_error declared str, assigned None on the
    success branch. Benign at runtime; should be str | None.

4.5 The judge's agreement figure is not yet computed
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
eval/drafting.py reports the Groq verdict rate but carries a note that
judge-human agreement is "reported separately once the drafts are hand-reviewed."
BUILD.md S6.3 is explicit that agreement is what makes the judge defensible
rather than decorative. Until the ~50 sampled drafts are hand-labelled, the
groundedness number should not be presented as validated.


================================================================================
5. SECURITY REVIEW
================================================================================

Checked and CLEAN:

  Prompt injection via email body — SAFE. Email text is passed as an ARGUMENT to
  str.format(), never as part of the template, so braces in a body are inert.
  Verified with bodies containing "{sops}", "{}", "{0}" and "{x}" — none raised
  or interpolated. (This is worth keeping in mind if anyone later switches to
  f-strings or .format on user-supplied templates, which would break it.)

  Label injection via the LLM baseline — SAFE. _parse matches replies against the
  known label set, so a model answering "tax_filing" cannot create a thirteenth
  class. Reasoning blocks (<think>...</think>) are stripped before parsing so a
  model's deliberation, which names several categories, cannot be mistaken for
  its conclusion.

  Placeholder fabrication — SAFE and deliberate. A draft containing a placeholder
  the vault never issued (e.g. [NRIC_7]) fails the draft rather than shipping a
  bare token. Covered by test_fabricated_placeholder_fails_the_draft.

  Secret handling — CLEAN. .env untracked and gitignored; env.py returns only
  variable NAMES, never values; key_status() reports booleans. No key is logged
  or serialised.

  Committed artefacts — CLEAN. All 11 JSON files under eval/results/ scanned for
  NRIC and SG phone patterns: zero hits.

Residual risks, both stated rather than fixed:

  - PII detection is regex plus a street gazetteer. Free-text addresses without a
    street-type token are the known gap. Recall is MEASURED (1.0000 on planted
    values) rather than claimed, which is the right posture — but planted PII is
    PII the generator knew to plant, so this measures detection of known shapes,
    not of everything a citizen might write.
  - See 3.3 — the module measuring containment currently writes raw values.


================================================================================
6. TEST COVERAGE
================================================================================

305 tests, 2,430 lines across 8 files. All passing.

    test_schemas.py ......... invariants, enums, redaction boundary
    test_router.py .......... escalation logic (highest-value)
    test_scrubber.py ........ PII detection and rehydration
    test_sop_corpus.py ...... corpus structure and validation
    test_graph_smoke.py ..... 11 — wiring, conditional edge, every class routes
    test_draft_failure.py ... 17 — the auto_reply_intended invariant
    test_calibration.py ..... rollup, monotonicity, ECE
    test_llm_zeroshot.py .... 17 — self-consistency, parsing, degradation

Gaps worth closing:

  - No test covers the multi-CITED case in 3.2. Add one alongside the fix.
  - No test asserts the reportability flag agrees with thresholds.yaml (3.1).
  - No test for pii_recall's serialisation (3.3).
  - No adversarial-length test for flags (4.1).

All four are regression tests for the defects above and should land with the
fixes rather than separately.


================================================================================
7. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MOST
================================================================================

Everything in sections 3 and 4 is localised and cheap. The real problem is
elsewhere and is not an architecture problem:

    macro-F1 (12 classes) ......... 0.6035
    oos_other_agency .............. F1 0.000 over 41 test examples
    payment ....................... F1 0.257
    coverage at <=10% risk ........ 2.3%

A class that is never once predicted correctly across 41 examples is a training
failure, not a weak class. Investigated and ruled out: label alignment is correct
(labels.json is sorted, matching train_encoder.py), and the splits are clean
(grouped by scenario_id, zero bleed). The signature is undertraining —
training.json shows calibration accuracy plateauing at epoch 3 (0.7357) and
FALLING at epoch 4 (0.7282) with train loss still at 0.98.

The consequence for the writeup is direct: coverage of 2.3% at a 10% risk
tolerance does not support a claim that a meaningful share of the inbox can be
automated. The mechanism is sound and well-tested; it is being fed weak
predictions.

Related, and awkward: the LLM zero-shot baseline currently BEATS the encoder.

                        encoder    llm 0-shot
    accuracy             0.667        0.833
    macro-F1             0.655        0.826
    ECE                  0.308        0.124
    sec/email            0.631        8.643
    distinct conf vals      36            2

(n=36 stratified, k=3. Subject to 3.4 — recompute with a fixed label set.)

The architectural argument survives: 2 distinct confidence values against 36 is
the resolution cap at 1/k, which no amount of data removes, and that is the real
case for an encoder when the threshold is the product. But "the encoder is better
calibrated" is currently FALSE as measured, and the writeup cannot assert it.
Either the classifier is retrained, or the model-selection section is rewritten
around the resolution/latency/cost argument and reports the accuracy gap
honestly.

One further note for the build log: the fitted temperature is 0.6831, which
SHARPENS rather than flattens. This is the opposite of BUILD.md S5.5's premise
that raw softmax is overconfident. The cause is the 12->5 rollup: probability
mass scattered across several classes within one bucket sums to an
UNDER-confident bucket score. Worth recording as a genuine finding — it is a
consequence of the bucket design that the design did not anticipate.


================================================================================
8. NOT BUILT — Stage 6, outside the backend

=== AUDIT ===
================================================================================
ARCHITECTURE AUDIT — Calibrated Triage Agent
================================================================================

Date:     2026-09-02
Scope:    Backend only. src/triage/, eval/, config/, tests/. Stage 6 deliverables
          (Streamlit, Docker, docs/) are not built and are listed in section 8
          rather than reported as defects.
Method:   Static (ruff, mypy), dynamic (287→305 pytest), and adversarial probing.
          Every finding below was reproduced at the command line; none is
          inferred from reading alone. Line numbers are as of this date.

Verified state at time of audit:
    ruff .................. all checks passed (src, eval, scripts, tests)
    pytest ................ 305 passed
    mypy .................. 13 errors, all cosmetic except one (see 4.4)
    test suite size ....... 2,430 lines across 8 files
    eval corpus ........... 520 test emails, 12 classes


================================================================================
1. SUMMARY
================================================================================

The architecture is sound. The layering the design argues for — corpus-derived
policy, a single escalation gate, calibration at bucket level, drafting as the
only fallible node — is implemented as described, and the invariants that matter
are enforced structurally rather than by convention.

Four real defects were found. None is a design flaw; all four are localised and
each is a few lines to fix. Two of them (3.1, 3.2) would produce a WRONG NUMBER
IN THE WRITEUP rather than a crash, which makes them the most serious kind of
bug this project can have — the failure mode BUILD.md's "eval/results/ is
committed" rule exists to prevent.

The dominant risk to the submission is not in this list. It is that the
classifier is undertrained (macro-F1 0.6035, one class at F1 0.000) while every
component around it is sound. See section 7.


================================================================================
2. WHAT IS COMPLETE AND VERIFIED
================================================================================

2.1 src/triage/schemas.py — 476 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The strongest file in the repository. Its distinguishing property is that the
routing invariants are enforced in pydantic validators rather than in the
router's control flow, so a future edit to route.py cannot violate them without
raising.

Verified enforced:
  - _always_escalate_buckets_escalate: REQUIRES_ACCOUNT_LOOKUP, HIGH_CONSEQUENCE
    and NO_SUPPORTING_SOP cannot construct a non-escalate decision at ANY
    confidence, including 1.0.
  - _reason_matches_action: an escalated item must carry a reason; a non-escalated
    one must not.
  - _redirect_only_for_out_of_scope: REDIRECT is unavailable to any other bucket,
    and AUTO_REPLY unavailable outside auto_answerable.
  - _check_distribution: probabilities must sum to 1.0 within 1e-3, and the
    predicted label must exist in the distribution.

The Email/ground-truth separation is correct and worth keeping. Email declares
extra="forbid", so a corpus row (which carries label, source_sops, plant_pii and
eight other generation fields) cannot be loaded as an Email. This is deliberate:
a real inbound citizen email has no `label` field, so if Email accepted extras a
node could read email.label, score perfectly in evaluation, and be impossible to
deploy. Forbidding extras converts that mistake into an immediate failure at the
seam instead of an inflated metric. eval/dataset.py holds ground truth in a
SIBLING object (Labelled.email / Labelled.label), so the runtime path cannot
reach it even accidentally.

redacted() is a genuine persistence boundary: it substitutes the scrubbed text,
empties the vault, drops the sender, and — importantly — falls back to blanking
the body entirely when scrubbing never ran, rather than passing the original
through on the assumption it was clean.

2.2 src/triage/graph.py — 232 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    scrub -> classify -> calibrate -> retrieve -> route -+-> draft    -> END
                                                         +-> declined -> END

Six nodes, one conditional edge, dependencies injected via GraphDeps so nodes
stay pure(state) -> partial state and tests construct graphs with stubs and no
weights on disk.

The conditional edge is the escalation gate made structural: an escalated item
does not reach the drafting node because NO EDGE LEADS THERE, not because of an
early return inside the drafter that a later edit could delete.

Fail-safe verified by injecting a classifier that raises:
    classifier crash -> escalate | no_supporting_sop | in_human_queue: True
    errors: ['classify failed: model died',
             'calibrate skipped: no classification',
             'retrieve skipped: no classification',
             'routed without a prediction: escalating']
    draft: not_attempted
Each node degrades independently, records why, and the item reaches a human.
Nothing guesses.

2.3 src/triage/nodes/route.py — 192 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Eight escalation reasons in documented precedence. Reasons 1-7 are structural and
would fire identically at probability 1.0; only reason 8 (low_confidence) reads
the model. The threshold clamp from BUILD.md S9.9 is intact — verified that a
sweep multiplier of 1.5 does not raise.

2.4 src/triage/nodes/calibrate.py — 124 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Contains the subtlest correct decision in the codebase, and it is worth stating
because it is easy to get wrong and impossible to notice when wrong:

    The predicted bucket is the bucket of the PREDICTED CLASS, not the argmax of
    the summed bucket distribution.

These differ. An email at account_specific 0.40 with three auto-answerable
classes at 0.20 each has an auto_answerable bucket mass of 0.60 — larger than
the 0.40 on the bucket that actually applies. Taking the argmax bucket would
auto-reply to an enquiry about a real taxpayer's record. The code follows the
class; test_rollup_follows_the_class_not_the_argmax_bucket pins it.

log(0) is guarded via _EPSILON for buckets holding no probability mass.

2.5 src/triage/pii/ — scrubber.py 171, nric.py 75
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - NRIC checksum verified against valid (S0433218J, G2720465T, S1234567D) and
    invalid (S0000000A, X1234567A, S123456D) inputs. All six correct.
  - Scrub recall on the test split: 1.0000 (127/127 planted values).
  - No PII in ANY committed file under eval/results/ — all 11 JSON files scanned
    for NRIC and SG phone patterns, zero hits.
  - .env is untracked and correctly matched by .gitignore line 7.
  - Rehydration happens in exactly one place (draft.py) and only after the
    network call.

2.6 src/triage/sop/ — loader.py 197, index.py 142
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
17 SOPs; 14 indexed, 3 held out (SOP-INC-001, SOP-INC-002, SOP-REL-005).
config/taxonomy.yaml vs corpus-derived buckets: ZERO mismatches across all 12
classes. The holdout works by derivation — an empty CLASS_TO_SOPS lookup IS the
no_supporting_sop signal, so holding out a further SOP needs no code change.

Loader validation is strict and fails at startup: missing frontmatter keys,
synthetic != true, empty intents, and empty references are all hard errors. The
synthetic banner check is a structural guard against the misrepresentation
failure mode, not decoration.

2.7 eval/ — 12 files, ~2,050 lines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Single entrypoint (run_eval.py) writing 11 committed artefacts plus 2 PNGs.

Split hygiene verified clean:
  - All three eval entrypoints default to --split test.
  - No reference to the "train" split anywhere in eval/ outside dataset.py.
  - Temperature is fitted on `calibration` (scripts/fit_calibration.py) and
    reported on `test` (run_eval.py). No crossover.

The risk-coverage sweep calls the REAL router at each of 37 multipliers rather
than reimplementing the decision rule, so the published curve cannot drift from
the system it describes. Classification runs once; only routing is re-run.

2.8 Structural walls
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Both walls BUILD.md S4.1 requires were checked by grep and hold:
  - src/ never imports scripts/ or eval/         (0 matches)
  - src/ never references OpenAI (paid, build-time only)  (0 matches)
The runtime therefore stays free-tier and reproducible on a grader's own key.

2.9 The two misfile guards (added this session)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
foreign_income_dta and scam_report were declared in SOP frontmatter but
unenforced. Both are now wired. Measured on the 520-email test split:

    foreign_income_signal   P 1.000   R 0.762   support 42
    scam_signal             P 1.000   R 0.976   support 42

Precision 1.000 on both means zero false positives, so they cost no coverage.
They are misfile guards rather than cross-cutting conditions: they matter only
when the classifier puts an email in the WRONG class, in the direction where
that error is unsafe (auto-answering a held-out foreign-income question from the
residency SOP; redirecting a fraud victim to another agency).

Note: these do NOT require retraining the classifier. flags.py is pure regex over
text and the router consults it after classification. The weights and the
12-class label set are untouched. This is BUILD.md S9.4's separation working as
intended — policy changes without a retrain.

hardship_or_waiver remains the only declared-but-unwired trigger, which is the
documented S10 deferral, and tests/test_schemas.py now asserts that every wired
flag keys on a trigger some indexed SOP actually declares.


================================================================================
3. REAL DEFECTS — fix before reporting any number
================================================================================

3.1 summary.json asserts reportability that config/thresholds.yaml denies
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEVERITY: high — this is the exact failure BUILD.md S7 exists to prevent.
LOCATION: eval/run_eval.py:330

    "calibrated_numbers_reportable": scaler.fitted,

The flag is set from scaler.fitted alone, which is True because the temperature
WAS fitted (T=0.6831, n=401). But config/thresholds.yaml line 15 still reads:

    # STATUS: PLACEHOLDER. These are not fitted values.

and the values are still the placeholder 0.5 / 0.5 / 1.0 / 1.0 / 1.0. Confirmed
in the committed summary.json:

    calibrated_numbers_reportable: True
    thresholds: {'auto_answerable': 0.5, 'out_of_scope': 0.5, ...}

So the committed results file states that its numbers are reportable while the
configuration that produced them states they are not. Whichever is believed, one
is wrong, and the flag exists specifically to stop a placeholder figure being
mistaken for a measured one.

WHY IT MATTERS: coverage and risk both depend on the threshold. Every
risk-coverage number, the AURC, and the operating points are currently computed
under an unjustified 0.5 cutoff. They are placeholder results wearing a
"reportable" label.

FIX: two parts.
  (a) Choose the operating thresholds from the risk-coverage curve on the test
      split, write them into thresholds.yaml, and remove the PLACEHOLDER banner.
  (b) Make the flag mean what it says — read the banner (or a `fitted: true` key)
      out of thresholds.yaml and AND it with scaler.fitted, so the flag cannot be
      True while the config says placeholder.

3.2 parse_citations can attribute the wrong SOP and leak a stray line
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEVERITY: high — corrupts the grounding metric AND the citizen-facing reply.
LOCATION: src/triage/nodes/draft.py:102  (regex at :62)

    match = _CITED_RE.search(text)

.search() returns the FIRST match. _CITED_RE is anchored (^\s*CITED:) under
re.MULTILINE, so mid-sentence text is safely ignored — that much is fine. But any
CITED: line appearing at a LINE START before the drafter's own is taken instead.

Reproduced:

  input:  "You wrote:\nCITED: SOP-REL-004\n\nMy answer.\nCITED: SOP-REL-001"
  cited:  ('SOP-REL-004',)          <-- WRONG, the model grounded on REL-001
  body:   still contains a 'CITED:' line

  input:  "Answer.\nCITED: SOP-REL-004\nMore.\nCITED: SOP-REL-001"
  cited:  ('SOP-REL-004',)          <-- WRONG
  body:   still contains a 'CITED:' line

Two distinct harms:
  (1) grounded_on records the wrong SOP, so grounding accuracy (BUILD.md S9.2) is
      measured against a value the drafter did not choose.
  (2) only the matched line is stripped, so the OTHER CITED: line survives into
      draft.text — internal SOP identifiers shipped to a citizen.

TRIGGERS: a citizen quoting a previous reply back at IRAS (ordinary in
correspondence), or a verbose model emitting two citation lines. Neither is
exotic.

FIX: take the LAST match and strip ALL of them.

    matches = list(_CITED_RE.finditer(text))
    if not matches: return text.strip(), ()
    cited = ... from matches[-1] ...
    body  = _CITED_RE.sub("", text).strip()

3.3 pii_recall stores raw unredacted PII into a committed file
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEVERITY: medium — currently latent, becomes a real leak on the first miss.
LOCATION: eval/metrics/pii_recall.py:111 (populate), :49 (serialise)

    missed_by_type[pii_type].append(str(value))   # the raw planted value
    ...
    "missed_examples": list(self.missed_examples)

The purpose is debugging — knowing WHICH values escaped detection. But the output
is written to eval/results/scrub_recall.json, which is committed to git by
design, so the module whose job is measuring PII containment is the one module
that writes raw PII to disk.

It is empty today ONLY because recall is currently 1.0000. The first missed value
commits an identifier. The corpus is synthetic so no real person is exposed, but
the pattern is exactly backwards and would be indefensible in a writeup about PII
handling.

FIX: store a masked form and keep the diagnostic value —
    "S0433218J" -> "S****218J", or record (type, length, first/last char).
Alternatively gate the raw list behind an explicit --debug-pii flag that never
writes to eval/results/.

3.4 encoder_vs_llm computes macro-F1 over a data-derived label set
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEVERITY: medium — makes the headline model-selection comparison unsound.
LOCATION: eval/ablations/encoder_vs_llm.py:87

    report = classification_report(truth, predicted)     # labels= omitted

With labels omitted, classification_report derives the label set from the union
of truth and predictions actually seen. On a small stratified sample the two
models see DIFFERENT label sets — a class the encoder never predicts but the LLM
does (or vice versa) changes the macro denominator — so the two macro-F1 figures
are averages over different numbers of classes and are not comparable.

Quantified:
    derived labels ('filing','payment')               -> macro_f1 0.3333
    fixed   labels ('filing','payment','tax_reliefs') -> macro_f1 0.2222
    discrepancy 0.1111 on the same predictions

This directly affects the encoder-vs-LLM table, which is the evidence for the
model-selection deliverable.

FIX: pass the fixed 12-class set to both calls —
    classification_report(truth, predicted, labels=tuple(encoder.labels))


================================================================================
4. LOWER-SEVERITY FINDINGS
================================================================================

4.1 Quadratic backtracking in the currency-question pattern
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION: src/triage/nodes/flags.py:71  (_CURRENCY_QUESTION)

NOTE — this corrects an earlier verbal report in which I attributed the slowdown
to _ACCOUNT_PATTERNS. Isolating each pattern individually shows the account
patterns are fast; _CURRENCY_QUESTION is the sole cause.

The [^.?!]* segments on either side of the first-person marker backtrack against
input with no sentence terminator. Measured on "my " * n + "refund?":

        n_words   seconds
            750     0.060
           1500     0.257
           3000     0.999
           6000     4.619

Clean quadratic — doubling the input quadruples the time. Real citizen emails are
~2KB and complete in milliseconds, so this is not a live problem; it is a
denial-of-service shape in a public-facing intake path, which is a different
thing from a bug.

FIX (cheapest): cap the text length before flag detection, e.g. detect_flags
operates on text[:4000]. A citizen email longer than that is already anomalous.
Alternatively bound the wildcards — [^.?!]{0,200} — which preserves intent, since
a first-person marker 200+ characters from the currency figure is not the
"whose facts" signal the pattern is trying to catch.

4.2 No minimum-content guard
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A one-character body ("x") flows through the whole pipeline and reaches
auto_reply if the classifier is confident. Verified with a stub forcing 0.9.

The real MiniLM would probably be unconfident on such input and the threshold
would catch it — but that is a hope about model behaviour, not a property. Every
other safety rule in this system is structural, and this one is not.

FIX: escalate below a minimum token count with a new reason (insufficient_content),
or document explicitly that the confidence threshold is the intended guard.

4.3 Dead code
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - TemperatureScaler.apply()  (models/calibration.py:57) — 0 call sites.
    nodes/calibrate.py reimplements the scaling inline, correctly, in log space.
    Having two implementations of the contribution's core transformation, one
    unused, invites a future edit to the wrong one. Either wire it or delete it.
  - Outcome.wrong_automation  (eval/metrics/risk_coverage.py:47) — defined, never
    called.
  - eval/dataset.py iter_splits — defined, used only in its own module.

4.4 mypy — 13 errors
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Twelve are cosmetic: missing generic parameters (StateGraph), torch functions
returning Any, and two unused type: ignore comments. One is a genuine annotation
mismatch:

    eval/drafting.py:181 — drafter_error declared str, assigned None on the
    success branch. Benign at runtime; should be str | None.

4.5 The judge's agreement figure is not yet computed
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
eval/drafting.py reports the Groq verdict rate but carries a note that
judge-human agreement is "reported separately once the drafts are hand-reviewed."
BUILD.md S6.3 is explicit that agreement is what makes the judge defensible
rather than decorative. Until the ~50 sampled drafts are hand-labelled, the
groundedness number should not be presented as validated.


================================================================================
5. SECURITY REVIEW
================================================================================

Checked and CLEAN:

  Prompt injection via email body — SAFE. Email text is passed as an ARGUMENT to
  str.format(), never as part of the template, so braces in a body are inert.
  Verified with bodies containing "{sops}", "{}", "{0}" and "{x}" — none raised
  or interpolated. (This is worth keeping in mind if anyone later switches to
  f-strings or .format on user-supplied templates, which would break it.)

  Label injection via the LLM baseline — SAFE. _parse matches replies against the
  known label set, so a model answering "tax_filing" cannot create a thirteenth
  class. Reasoning blocks (<think>...</think>) are stripped before parsing so a
  model's deliberation, which names several categories, cannot be mistaken for
  its conclusion.

  Placeholder fabrication — SAFE and deliberate. A draft containing a placeholder
  the vault never issued (e.g. [NRIC_7]) fails the draft rather than shipping a
  bare token. Covered by test_fabricated_placeholder_fails_the_draft.

  Secret handling — CLEAN. .env untracked and gitignored; env.py returns only
  variable NAMES, never values; key_status() reports booleans. No key is logged
  or serialised.

  Committed artefacts — CLEAN. All 11 JSON files under eval/results/ scanned for
  NRIC and SG phone patterns: zero hits.

Residual risks, both stated rather than fixed:

  - PII detection is regex plus a street gazetteer. Free-text addresses without a
    street-type token are the known gap. Recall is MEASURED (1.0000 on planted
    values) rather than claimed, which is the right posture — but planted PII is
    PII the generator knew to plant, so this measures detection of known shapes,
    not of everything a citizen might write.
  - See 3.3 — the module measuring containment currently writes raw values.


================================================================================
6. TEST COVERAGE
================================================================================

305 tests, 2,430 lines across 8 files. All passing.

    test_schemas.py ......... invariants, enums, redaction boundary
    test_router.py .......... escalation logic (highest-value)
    test_scrubber.py ........ PII detection and rehydration
    test_sop_corpus.py ...... corpus structure and validation
    test_graph_smoke.py ..... 11 — wiring, conditional edge, every class routes
    test_draft_failure.py ... 17 — the auto_reply_intended invariant
    test_calibration.py ..... rollup, monotonicity, ECE
    test_llm_zeroshot.py .... 17 — self-consistency, parsing, degradation

Gaps worth closing:

  - No test covers the multi-CITED case in 3.2. Add one alongside the fix.
  - No test asserts the reportability flag agrees with thresholds.yaml (3.1).
  - No test for pii_recall's serialisation (3.3).
  - No adversarial-length test for flags (4.1).

All four are regression tests for the defects above and should land with the
fixes rather than separately.


================================================================================
7. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MOST
================================================================================

Everything in sections 3 and 4 is localised and cheap. The real problem is
elsewhere and is not an architecture problem:

    macro-F1 (12 classes) ......... 0.6035
    oos_other_agency .............. F1 0.000 over 41 test examples
    payment ....................... F1 0.257
    coverage at <=10% risk ........ 2.3%

A class that is never once predicted correctly across 41 examples is a training
failure, not a weak class. Investigated and ruled out: label alignment is correct
(labels.json is sorted, matching train_encoder.py), and the splits are clean
(grouped by scenario_id, zero bleed). The signature is undertraining —
training.json shows calibration accuracy plateauing at epoch 3 (0.7357) and
FALLING at epoch 4 (0.7282) with train loss still at 0.98.

The consequence for the writeup is direct: coverage of 2.3% at a 10% risk
tolerance does not support a claim that a meaningful share of the inbox can be
automated. The mechanism is sound and well-tested; it is being fed weak
predictions.

Related, and awkward: the LLM zero-shot baseline currently BEATS the encoder.

                        encoder    llm 0-shot
    accuracy             0.667        0.833
    macro-F1             0.655        0.826
    ECE                  0.308        0.124
    sec/email            0.631        8.643
    distinct conf vals      36            2

(n=36 stratified, k=3. Subject to 3.4 — recompute with a fixed label set.)

The architectural argument survives: 2 distinct confidence values against 36 is
the resolution cap at 1/k, which no amount of data removes, and that is the real
case for an encoder when the threshold is the product. But "the encoder is better
calibrated" is currently FALSE as measured, and the writeup cannot assert it.
Either the classifier is retrained, or the model-selection section is rewritten
around the resolution/latency/cost argument and reports the accuracy gap
honestly.

One further note for the build log: the fitted temperature is 0.6831, which
SHARPENS rather than flattens. This is the opposite of BUILD.md S5.5's premise
that raw softmax is overconfident. The cause is the 12->5 rollup: probability
mass scattered across several classes within one bucket sums to an
UNDER-confident bucket score. Worth recording as a genuine finding — it is a
consequence of the bucket design that the design did not anticipate.

    app/streamlit_app.py .......... the officer's two-queue demo
    Dockerfile, .dockerignore ..... clean-machine reproducibility
    docs/DEVELOPMENT_NARRATIVE.md
    docs/MODEL_SELECTION.md ....... should absorb section 7's finding
    docs/DEPLOYMENT.md
    docs/LIMITATIONS.md ........... should absorb 4.1, 4.2, 5's residual risks

the openai/gpt-oss-* models also on the roster because GPT-4o generated the
corpus and a judge from the generator's family would weaken separation rule 3.

================================================================================

    2.  3.2  parse_citations last-match + strip all        (wrong metric + leak)
    3.  3.4  fixed label set in encoder_vs_llm             (blocks model selection)

    7.  4.3  resolve dead code

Items 1-3 are prerequisites for reporting anything. Item 4 determines whether

"""LangGraph assembly -- the pipeline, wired.

RUNTIME. The one place the node order is stated, and the only module that knows
about all of them.

::

    scrub -> classify -> calibrate -> retrieve -> route -+-> draft    -> END
                                                         |
                                                         +-> declined -> END

LangGraph rather than a plain function chain, for one reason that pays off in this
domain: the execution path is a declared graph rather than an implicit consequence
of control flow, so "what happened to this email" is answerable by reading the
edges. High-stakes auditable workflows favour constrained patterns whose path is
traceable end to end (``BUILD.md`` S3).

**The conditional edge is the escalation gate made structural.** An escalated item
does not reach the drafting node at all -- not by an early return inside the drafter,
which a later edit could remove, but because no edge leads there. The router is the
single place that decision is made.

**Dependencies are injected at build time, not imported by the nodes.** The
classifier, SOP index, temperature and thresholds are bound into the graph by
:func:`build_graph`, so the ablation harness swaps a classifier or a temperature
without touching a node, and tests construct a graph with fakes and no model on
disk. A node that reached for a global would make both impossible.

**State merges rather than replaces.** Each node returns only the fields it sets;
``TriageState`` accumulates them, so a completed state is the full audit record of
one decision -- which is what the demo renders and what every metric reads.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Mapping
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Final

from langgraph.graph import END, StateGraph

from triage.llm.client import LLMClient, LLMError
from triage.models.base import Classifier
from triage.models.calibration import TemperatureScaler
from triage.nodes.calibrate import calibrate_node
from triage.nodes.classify import classify_node
from triage.nodes.draft import draft_node
from triage.nodes.flags import detect_flags
from triage.nodes.retrieve import retrieve_node
from triage.nodes.route import load_thresholds, route
from triage.nodes.scrub import scrub_node
from triage.schemas import (
    Action,
    Bucket,
    DraftResult,
    DraftStatus,
    EscalationReason,
    RoutingDecision,
    TriageState,
)
from triage.sop.index import SOPIndex, build_index

#: Confidence recorded when the pipeline could not produce one. The item escalates,
#: so the value is never compared against a threshold; 0.0 is the honest record of
#: "no confidence was obtained" rather than a score that might be read as measured.
_NO_CONFIDENCE: Final[float] = 0.0


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GraphDeps:
    """Everything the nodes need, resolved once at startup.

    Assembled here rather than loaded per email: the SOP corpus is parsed and
    validated once, the classifier holds its weights, and the thresholds are read
    from config. A per-email reload would put a file-system error on the path of a
    citizen's enquiry.
    """

    classifier: Classifier
    index: SOPIndex
    scaler: TemperatureScaler
    thresholds: Mapping[str, float]
    client: LLMClient | None = None
    multiplier: float = 1.0

    @property
    def bucket_of(self) -> Mapping[str, str]:
        """class -> bucket, derived from SOP frontmatter."""
        return self.index.bucket


def _route_node(state: TriageState, deps: GraphDeps) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Detect flags and make the escalation decision.

    Flag detection sits here rather than in its own node because it is an input to
    exactly one decision and has no other consumer -- a separate node would add a
    graph edge that never branches.

    An item that reached this point without a bucket score never got a usable
    prediction. It escalates as ``no_supporting_sop``: the pipeline has no grounds
    to act, and failing toward the officer is the only safe direction.
    """
    if state.bucket_score is None:
        return {
            "decision": RoutingDecision(
                action=Action.ESCALATE,
                bucket=Bucket.NO_SUPPORTING_SOP,
                confidence=_NO_CONFIDENCE,
                reason=EscalationReason.NO_SUPPORTING_SOP,
                calibrated=deps.scaler.fitted,
            ),
            "errors": [*state.errors, "routed without a prediction: escalating"],
        }

    text = state.scrub.text if state.scrub else state.email.text
    flags = detect_flags(text, state.classification)
    sops = tuple(deps.index.by_id[sid] for sid in state.sop_ids if sid in deps.index.by_id)

    decision = route(
        state.bucket_score,
        sops,
        flags,
        dict(deps.thresholds),
        calibrated=deps.scaler.fitted,
        multiplier=deps.multiplier,
    )
    return {"decision": decision}


def _should_draft(state: TriageState) -> str:
    """The conditional edge: only an item the router acted on reaches the drafter."""
    return "draft" if state.auto_reply_intended else "declined"


def _not_attempted(state: TriageState) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Record that drafting was declined rather than skipped.

    An escalated item never reaches the drafting node -- that is the escalation gate
    being structural rather than a branch inside the drafter. But its ``draft``
    field must still be populated, because ``None`` is ambiguous: it reads equally
    as "the router declined" and as "the run stopped early". ``NOT_ATTEMPTED`` says
    which, so drafting availability counts only items drafting was actually asked
    for (``BUILD.md`` S5.8).
    """
    return {"draft": DraftResult(status=DraftStatus.NOT_ATTEMPTED, sop_ids=state.sop_ids)}


def build_graph(deps: GraphDeps) -> Any:
    """Compile the triage graph.

    Nodes are bound to ``deps`` here, so each remains ``pure(state) -> partial
    state`` and stays independently testable without a graph.
    """
    builder: StateGraph = StateGraph(TriageState)

    builder.add_node("scrub", scrub_node)
    builder.add_node("classify", lambda s: classify_node(s, deps.classifier))
    builder.add_node("calibrate", lambda s: calibrate_node(s, deps.bucket_of, deps.scaler))
    builder.add_node("retrieve", lambda s: retrieve_node(s, deps.index))
    builder.add_node("route", lambda s: _route_node(s, deps))
    builder.add_node("draft", lambda s: draft_node(s, deps.index, deps.client))
    builder.add_node("declined", _not_attempted)

    builder.set_entry_point("scrub")
    builder.add_edge("scrub", "classify")
    builder.add_edge("classify", "calibrate")
    builder.add_edge("calibrate", "retrieve")
    builder.add_edge("retrieve", "route")
    builder.add_conditional_edges(
        "route", _should_draft, {"draft": "draft", "declined": "declined"}
    )
    builder.add_edge("draft", END)
    builder.add_edge("declined", END)

    return builder.compile()


def build_default_deps(
    *,
    classifier: Classifier | None = None,
    drafting: bool = True,
    multiplier: float = 1.0,
) -> GraphDeps:
    """Assemble dependencies from what is on disk.

    Args:
        classifier: Overrides the fine-tuned encoder, for ablations and tests.
        drafting: When False, no LLM client is constructed. Every auto-reply then
            records a drafting failure, which is the correct behaviour for a
            routing-only eval sweep: the routing decision is unaffected, and
            drafting availability reports the absence honestly.
        multiplier: Scales every threshold. Swept to trace the risk-coverage curve.

    A missing ``GEMINI_API_KEY`` is not fatal. The item escalates to the officer
    carrying its SOP, exactly as a rate limit would -- the designed failure path
    rather than a special case (``BUILD.md`` S5.8).
    """
    if classifier is None:
        from triage.models.encoder import EncoderClassifier

        classifier = EncoderClassifier()

    client: LLMClient | None = None
    if drafting:
        from triage.llm.client import GeminiClient

        try:
            client = GeminiClient()
        except LLMError:
            client = None

    return GraphDeps(
        classifier=classifier,
        index=build_index(),
        scaler=TemperatureScaler.load(),
        thresholds=load_thresholds(),
        client=client,
        multiplier=multiplier,
    )


def run_one(graph: Any, state: TriageState) -> TriageState:
    """Run one email through a compiled graph and return the completed state.

    LangGraph returns the accumulated state as a mapping; it is validated back into
    a :class:`TriageState` so callers always receive the typed object.
    """
    result = graph.invoke(state)
    return result if isinstance(result, TriageState) else TriageState.model_validate(result)


__all__ = ["GraphDeps", "build_default_deps", "build_graph", "run_one"]

=== thresholds.yaml ===
# PER-BUCKET ESCALATION THRESHOLDS
#
# The escalation policy, readable in one file and diffable in git. Changing a
# number here changes system behaviour without touching code, which is the point:
# an operator should be able to argue with this file.
#
# THRESHOLDS ARE PER BUCKET, NOT PER CLASS. At 1,800 emails a bucket carries ~108
# test examples against ~45 for a class, and a threshold set on 45 examples is not
# defensible -- the binomial confidence interval is wider than the effect being
# measured. Each number goes where its data supports it.
#
# Only two of the five thresholds actually bite. Three buckets escalate regardless
# of confidence, so their value is recorded for completeness and never consulted.
#
# STATUS: PLACEHOLDER. These are not fitted values. Calibration is fitted on the
# calibration split by scripts/fit_calibration.py, and the operating points are
# chosen from the risk-coverage curve on the test split. No number produced under
# these placeholders may be reported (BUILD.md S7). RoutingDecision.calibrated
# carries the distinction forward so a placeholder result cannot be mistaken for a
# measured one.

buckets:
  auto_answerable:
    threshold: 0.5
    bites: true
    justification: >
      The only bucket where the agent asserts substantive tax content to a citizen,
      so this is the threshold that governs the coverage/error trade-off and the
      one the risk-coverage curve is swept over. Placeholder pending calibration.

  out_of_scope:
    threshold: 0.5
    bites: true
    justification: >
      Redirects auto-reply, so a low-confidence redirect would send a citizen to
      the wrong agency -- a visible, citizen-facing failure rather than an internal
      one. The threshold exists to make an uncertain redirect escalate instead.
      Placeholder pending calibration.

  requires_account_lookup:
    threshold: 1.0
    bites: false
    justification: >
      Never auto-replies. Answering requires reading a specific taxpayer's record,
      which the agent cannot do and must not guess at. Recorded as 1.0 for
      completeness; the router escalates on the bucket before any threshold is
      consulted.

  high_consequence:
    threshold: 1.0
    bites: false
    justification: >
      Never auto-replies. Financial distress and active fraud carry consequences no
      confidence score should be permitted to authorise an automated answer for.
      Recorded as 1.0 for completeness; never consulted.

  no_supporting_sop:
    threshold: 1.0
    bites: false
    justification: >
      Never auto-replies, and derived rather than hand-mapped: the class resolved
      to no indexed SOP, so there is nothing to ground a reply on. Recorded as 1.0
      for completeness; never consulted.

# The risk-coverage curve is generated by sweeping a global multiplier over every
# threshold above, using the real router rather than a reimplementation of it, so
# the curve cannot drift from the system it describes.
sweep:
  multiplier_min: 0.2

######## SCRUB NODE ########
"""Scrub node -- the gate every external call passes through.

RUNTIME. First node in the graph, deliberately: it runs before the classifier and
before any LLM call, so no node downstream of it ever sees a real identifier.

The node is a thin wrapper over :class:`triage.pii.scrubber.Scrubber`. The logic
lives there because it is also exercised by the scrub-recall metric and by the
scrub ablation, neither of which builds a graph.

**Failing open is the wrong default here.** If scrubbing raises, the state records
the error and carries the *unscrubbed* text nowhere: ``scrub`` stays ``None``, which
``TriageState.redacted`` reads as "never scrubbed" and blanks the body entirely
rather than assuming it was clean. The item then escalates, because a state with no
classification cannot route.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from functools import lru_cache

from triage.pii.scrubber import Scrubber
from triage.schemas import ScrubRecord, TriageState


@lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def _scrubber() -> Scrubber:
    """One shared scrubber. Compiling the pattern set per email is pure waste, and
    the object is stateless across calls -- each scrub returns its own vault."""
    return Scrubber()


def scrub_node(state: TriageState) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Replace PII with placeholders before anything else touches the text."""
    try:
        result = _scrubber().scrub(state.email.text)
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 -- recorded, never swallowed
        return {"errors": [*state.errors, f"scrub failed: {exc}"]}

    return {
        "scrub": ScrubRecord(text=result.text, vault=result.vault, counts=result.counts),
    }


__all__ = ["scrub_node"]
